items.title: Your RAG system is a retrieval problem
items.excerpt: Nine times out of ten the model is not hallucinating — it was handed the wrong three chunks. Fix the index before you touch the prompt.
items.standfirst: Nine times out of ten the model is not hallucinating. It was handed the wrong three chunks, and it did what it was built to do.
items.intro: Every retrieval system I have been asked to rescue was described to me as a model problem. It almost never is. The model wrote a confident paragraph because a confident paragraph is the only thing it could do with the three bad passages it was given.

sections.heading: The symptom
sections.body:
You ask a question you already know the answer to. The system answers something adjacent — right vocabulary, wrong specifics — and cites a document that mentions your keywords in passing.

The tell is the citation. Open the cited source. If the answer is not in there, you have a retrieval failure wearing a generation failure's clothes.

sections.heading: Chunk on meaning
sections.body:
Fixed-width chunking is convenient and almost always wrong. A ticket has a resolution; a contract has clauses. Cut on the seam the document already has.

Overlap is a patch for a bad boundary, not a strategy.
sections.quote: A chunk should be the smallest passage that would satisfy a reader who saw nothing else.

sections.heading: Filter before you rank
sections.body: Metadata filters are unglamorous and they outperform every reranker I have benchmarked. Apply them first and the reranker receives a shortlist worth ranking.

sections.heading: Measure the halves apart
sections.body: Grade retrieval separately from generation: known-good sources, recall at five, run nightly. If recall is healthy and the answers are still wrong, then — and only then — you have a model problem.

items.notes:
Log the retrieved passages alongside every answer. Storage is cheaper than the argument.
Recall at five, not at one — readers see three suggestions.

items.title: Star schemas still win
items.excerpt: One-big-table is a storage answer to a modelling question. A dimensional model still explains itself to an analyst who joined last week.
items.standfirst: One-big-table is a storage answer to a modelling question.
items.intro: Every few years someone announces that dimensional modelling is obsolete because storage is cheap. Storage was never the point. The point was that a new analyst could look at the model and understand the business.

sections.heading: What the wide table costs
sections.body: A single wide table is fast to build and fast to query. It is also a thousand columns nobody can explain, with grain that changes halfway down.

sections.heading: What the star buys
sections.body: Facts at a declared grain, dimensions that mean one thing each. The model documents itself, and questions have an obvious place to start.
sections.quote: A model is a description of the business that happens to be queryable.

sections.heading: Use both
sections.body: Build the star; publish wide tables from it for the dashboards that want them. The wide table is an output, not a foundation.

items.title: Reading an execution plan without fear
items.excerpt: The plan is not an oracle, it is a story about how the engine intends to spend its time. Here is the order I read it in.
items.standfirst: The plan is a story about how the engine intends to spend its time.
items.intro: Execution plans look like they were designed to be ignored. They reward about ten minutes of attention with most of what you need to know about a slow query.

sections.heading: Start at the bottom
sections.body: Read from the leaves: which tables are scanned, and how much of each. A full scan of a large table is usually the whole story.

sections.heading: Find the row explosion
sections.body: Look for the join where estimated rows jump by orders of magnitude. That is almost always a missing join key or a grain mismatch.

sections.heading: Then, and only then, tune
sections.body: Clustering, pruning and materialisation all help — after the query is asking the right question.
sections.quote: Most slow queries are wrong queries that happen to finish.

items.title: What I check before trusting a dashboard
items.excerpt: Row counts, a freshness stamp, and one number I can verify by hand. If a dashboard cannot survive those three, it is decoration.
items.standfirst: Three checks, five minutes, before any number goes in a deck.
items.intro: Before I quote a number from a dashboard I have not built, I spend five minutes on three checks. They have saved me more embarrassment than any tool.

sections.heading: Freshness
sections.body: When was this last loaded? If the dashboard does not say, that is the first finding.

sections.heading: Row counts
sections.body: Does the total roughly match the source? An order-of-magnitude gap means a join or a filter is wrong.

sections.heading: One number by hand
sections.body: Pick one figure and reproduce it from raw data. If you cannot, nobody else can either.
